When I started finding my way back into pure mathematics, my wife asked me a fair question: "Why are you doing that when it has nothing to do with Aigora?"
She had a point. I run Aigora, a boutique enterprise AI services company. There were clients to serve and products to build. No customer was asking me to prove a theorem in differential geometry.
The honest answer was, because I was curious.
I finished my doctorate in differential geometry at UC Santa Barbara in 2004. But then I went into computational neuroscience, and my last math paper, written with Guofang Wei, my PhD advisor, appeared in Geometry & Topology in 2010. After that I moved into statistics, data science, and building Aigora within the world of sensory science in which I grew up. Pure mathematics still mattered to me, and I still thought of myself as a mathematician, but it wasn't my daily work.
A specific set of reports pulled me back. In January 2026, a writeup of Erdős Problem #728 described GPT-5.2 Pro working with Harmonic's Aristotle to produce a Lean-checked proof. Then, on May 20, OpenAI announced that an internal model had disproved the longstanding grid-optimality conjecture in Erdős's planar unit-distance problem. Serious mathematicians had checked the argument.
That got my attention. It also left me with a practical question. How well did this work outside big labs and their private models? The reports showed what was possible at the frontier. They did not tell me what an independent researcher could reproduce with models I could actually access, or what the denominator looked like: failed attempts, plausible false proofs, human steering, and the work required to turn an answer into mathematics.
I had built my own workflow (Elves) using coding agents, parallel critics, numerical experiments, and adversarial review. I didn't want another benchmark. I wanted to put that workflow on a real problem that would punish a shallow answer, with a professional mathematician judging the result.
On May 26, 2026, I emailed Guofang and asked what problem she would work on if she had more time. She sent me one about the fundamental gap of a large ball in hyperbolic space.
The fundamental gap is the difference between the first two Dirichlet eigenvalues of a domain. Think of those eigenvalues as the first two natural frequencies of a drum, although the drum now lives in a negatively curved space. For a large hyperbolic ball of radius r, Guofang wanted the coefficient of the 1/r³ term in that gap.
I acknowledged the question at 4:23 that afternoon. At 5:46, about 84 minutes later, I sent back a proposed answer:
λ₂(Bᵣⁿ) − λ₁(Bᵣⁿ) = 4π² / ((n − 1)r³) + o(r⁻³)
The workflow had found the right way to represent the problem, connected a dimension-shift identity to an asymptotic expansion written elsewhere in the literature, and finished the calculation before I would have finished searching for the relevant papers. But speed didn't settle the mathematics. The first useful act after producing the answer was to hand it to someone qualified to doubt it.
A Proof Spine Is Not a Paper
The ball calculation led immediately to a larger question. What could we say about the fundamental gap for a general horoconvex domain in hyperbolic space? Horoconvexity is stronger than ordinary convexity — the boundary has to curve inward more sharply. That extra strength matters, because ordinary convexity in negative curvature is too weak to control the gap by diameter alone.
The target we settled on was modest and precise. For a horoconvex domain of large diameter D, we wanted to show that the gap could not shrink faster than order 1/D³. Not a sharp constant, not an extremality theorem — just the correct polynomial scale for large domains. The genuine difficulty was geometric: a large horoconvex domain can depart substantially from a perfect ball, and the argument has to keep that departure controlled while isolating the small effect that actually sets the gap. The ball calculation was this same problem with the hard coupling stripped out.
Within about two days, the AI workflow had produced a proof spine. By May 31, I had sent Guofang a complete draft. It repeated arguments, changed notation, defined objects after using them, and sometimes hid necessary details while making the prose smoother. I built a proof-explainer application to navigate it — but if a paper needs custom software to be understood, it isn't ready.
Guofang brought her husband, Xianzhe Dai, into the project after he had already begun checking the proof with her. She also invited Hien Nguyen, her previous collaborator on the opposite side of the problem, the matching large-diameter upper bound.
Guofang kept looking for simpler routes through the analytic core, and later supplied an exponential-decay simplification that changed how a major part of the proof should be presented. Xianzhe pushed on the architecture and readability of the argument. Hien challenged a low-dimensional proposition, worked through the dimension shift, supplied a radial-height diagram, and became a demanding structural editor. She identified exactly the kind of manuscript debt that AI can accumulate: repeated proofs, inconsistent notation, missing definitions, and simplification that removes the very details a reader needs.
One episode captures the division of labor. After Guofang found the simplifying idea, Claude Fable carried out a large rewrite. Then GPT-5.5 found a genuine weakness in the boundary-slope estimate. Fixing it required a low-energy Jost expansion, not another round of smoother prose.
The paper, by Xianzhe Dai, me, Xuan Hien Nguyen, and Guofang Wei, was submitted to arXiv on June 10. It is titled "A Large-Diameter Fundamental-Gap Lower Bound for Horoconvex Domains," and it's now in preparation for peer-reviewed publication. My first math paper in 16 years!
The calculation took 84 minutes, the proof spine about two days, and the draft about five. Making the mathematics defensible and clear took longer and is still work in progress.
The Humans Changed the Proof
The professional reaction developed in stages. The first calculation produced real surprise. By the first complete draft, the result looked genuinely worth publishing and reached a bound that experts had expected but had not proved. But belief in the theorem was not belief in the manuscript.
The same mathematicians who thought the result was good initially couldn't understand the early notes. The central operator was opaque. The analytic core quoted unfamiliar machinery without explaining why it was there. By June 6, the main argument occupied roughly 35 pages, yet its key idea was hard to see. After another reorganization it grew past 40 pages. Even after the readers had acquired a global picture, they thought the proof needed to be rebuilt around that picture.
They treated the output as research, not as a demonstration. They challenged the dimension shift, divided technical lemmas according to their own specialties, replaced a complicated estimate with a sharper known bound, checked boundary conditions and signs, and objected when a critical dimension was handled by pages of separate machinery. They wanted the paper to begin with the map between the ball and the domain, then organize the estimates by purpose and handle the dimensions through one idea where possible.
The AI drafts preserved the order of discovery. They accumulated every successful detour and gave the main idea the same weight as its scaffolding. A paper has to show which object matters, which estimate carries the argument, and why the hypotheses are there.
Their judgment was neither that AI had solved the problem nor that it had produced nonsense. It had found real mathematics and a path to a proof, but it had not recognized the most economical proof or explained the argument in a form a mathematician would naturally read. Turning that path into a paper required new ideas, simplification, restructuring, and line-by-line mathematical custody.
By July 1, I had concluded that AI could generate candidate mathematics faster than we could responsibly absorb it. Mathematicians might have more work to do, not less.
Speed Needs Brakes
On May 30 and May 31, I posted publicly about the project and shared the abstract on X. On June 9, SangHyun Park posted a preprint deriving the same D⁻³ scale through a different asymptotic route. His paper noted our public announcement, and I suspect my abstract was simply given to GPT-5.5 Pro for a proof, which is of course much easier than finding a proof of something you don't know is true or false. But who knows, and it doesn't matter. Our paper was submitted the next day regardless.
Then Speed Stopped Helping
Guofang had also given me a much harder problem, which remains open. After the priority experience, I am not publishing the conjecture or its surviving proof routes here. This second problem showed where speed stopped helping.
We tried to prove it while searching for counterexamples. We derived identities, built simplified models, and designed computations to kill attractive intermediate claims. Every useful statement went into a claims ledger with a status and source. Failed routes stayed in the record so that a fresh model could not rediscover them as new.
Coding agents worked directly in the repository, calling outside models, running checks, rendering diagrams, and assembling review packets. Overnight runs might produce a promising lemma, a counterexample, or six hours of work on the wrong statement. Every run needed a handoff recording what changed, what remained open, and where the evidence lived.
By July 20, the ledger contained more than 330 recorded call groups. Some represented one response, others a review swarm.
Git gives a different measure of the scale. From the repository's first commit on May 26 through July 20, the project accumulated 3,454 unique commits across its branches. During the most intense 21-day stretch, from June 14 through July 4, there were 2,143 commits, more than 100 per day.
That number is not a quality metric. It is a custody metric. A commit might contain a proposed lemma, a counterexample, a computation, a hostile review, a repaired certificate, or a durable record that an attractive idea had failed.
At one point I kept an Elves run alive for 12 straight days. Its ride-along feature let me give it new information and redirect it without ending the run or throwing away its working memory. Twelve days is 288 hours of wall-clock orchestration. We often had several agents running at once, so using an average concurrency of three, that one stretch represented roughly 864 agent-hours.
That is not 864 hours of pure model inference, much less 864 GPU-hours. It includes literature searches, model calls, local calculations, code execution, API delays, review, and the writing of artifacts that made the work auditable. But it is still a useful correction to the idea that an AI proof arrives as one answer to one prompt.
The first two entries in the July prove-or-disprove run were apparent full proofs, one from Gemini and one from Grok. Both failed local checks.
Models often produced a global-looking proof by weakening a quantifier, making a local statement uniform, transferring a simplified model to the original problem, or turning an averaged estimate into pointwise control. A proof could survive five favorable reviews because every reviewer inherited the same hidden assumption.
A passing vote meant only that a reviewer had not found a defect under the supplied context. Model agreement never counted as proof.
We proved special cases, derived useful identities, and killed attractive but false routes. The problem is much narrower, but it is not solved.
Ranking the Models
Based on my experience, in the context of differential geometry, here is how the models performed:
5.6 Sol — Best at proof architecture and final repair. It saw the whole chain of a proof, found wrong scales, detected stale targets and silent changes of scope, and repaired our AlphaEvolve evaluator. Its characteristic failure: perfecting a rigorous argument for a statement narrower than the theorem we meant to prove.
Claude Fable 5 — Best at deep derivation and long rewrites. It carried human ideas through measures, endpoints, constants, and dozens of pages, and rebuilt the public proof after Guofang's simplification. Its most elegant derivations sometimes depended on one beautiful but unproved global claim.
Sakana Fugu Ultra — Best at hostile review. It checked signs, conventions, integration by parts, quantifiers, certificates, and hidden upgrades with unusual persistence. But it was slow and literal; missing context could turn a convention question into a false alarm.
Kimi K3 — Best at original mechanisms. It proposed the strangest and sometimes most promising transformations and auxiliary objects, and produced the clean Mandarin factorization. But it invented terms, used estimates outside their hypotheses, or renamed the missing theorem as a lemma; long runs sometimes returned no answer.
GPT-5.5 Pro — Best at exact local criticism. It found a real weakness in the boundary-slope estimate of the public paper, forcing us to replace a handwave with a low-energy Jost expansion. Expensive, with less evidence of broad proof design than 5.6 Sol or Fable.
Gemini 3.1 Pro — Best at conservative algebra and adjudication. It recovered exact identities, checked scope, and gave reliable second opinions on bounded claims. It also produced an apparent full proof that failed local checks and initially endorsed a bad repair before reversing.
Grok 4.5 — Best at concise skepticism. It caught overclaims, missing uniformity, and conclusions stronger than their certificates. It missed some range restrictions and once shared a bad factor with another reviewer.
Muse Spark 1.1 — Best at independent long-context review. It added useful diversity and produced a serious alternative blueprint after calibration. It missed a numerical-certificate defect that 5.6 Sol found and could spend its output budget without reaching a verdict.
GLM 5.2 — Best at cheap substitutions and route critique. It occasionally found exactly the simplifying change of variables we needed, but too many empty or truncated calls made it undependable for custody of a proof.
Qwen 3.7 Max — Best at cheap dissent and bounded derivations. It helped kill an attractive intermediate claim and completed the open-ended language runs reliably, but made exact algebra, answer-lock, and quantifier errors that required symbolic replay.
DeepSeek V3.2 — Best at routine secondary checks. It handled ordinary calculations and supplied another vote cheaply, but was too agreeable and too lightly represented in the record to trust on hard gates.
Gemini 3.5 Flash — Best at editing and transcription. Fast at cleanup, image-assisted commentary, and low-cost sanity checks, but weak on delicate proof algebra and too willing to promote a scout into a claim.
K3 also taught me that more context is not always better. On three full-corpus calls it consumed 65,536 completion tokens without visible text. Give it the whole project and it could disappear into thought. Give it a distilled 1,000-token problem map and it could be excellent.
By task, I would recommend K3 for invention, 5.6 Sol for proof architecture, Fable for deep derivation and long rewrites, and Fugu for hostile review. Gemini, Grok, and Qwen were useful for cheap bounded checks when the algebra could be replayed. For computational discovery, AlphaEvolve with a deterministic evaluator often beat another chat model, but only after 5.6 Sol and a human audited the evaluator.
The team I settled on was simple. K3 proposes. Fable develops. 5.6 Sol repairs. Fugu attacks.
When Prompting Stopped Working
When ordinary prompting stopped helping, I tried evolutionary search, images, other languages, and fine-tuning.
AlphaEvolve
AlphaEvolve searched programs that scored candidate formulas, profiles, and finite-dimensional configurations. It did not read the theorem and prove it.
Our first evaluator used the wrong scaling, admitted invalid candidates, and mislabeled results. 5.6 Sol found the defects. After repair, AlphaEvolve rediscovered exact formulas, found near misses, generated adversarial cases, and stress-tested claims.
A generated program mattered only after local replay and mathematical interpretation. An optimizer exploits the score you wrote, not the theorem you meant.
Thinking in Pictures and Video
We gave Gemini Pro and Gemini Flash geometric diagrams and residual plots. The images suggested mechanisms and failure regions that had not been obvious in the equations. The strongest visual intuition was wrong, and another survived only in a narrow parameter range. The images were useful because they made false ideas specific enough to test.
Thinking in Other Languages
We tested whether asking K3 and Qwen to reason in Mandarin would help. We translated and randomized a controlled set of questions and ran three repetitions in each language.
In an early experiment, K3 answered seven of eight cases correctly in English and eight of eight in Mandarin. The first Mandarin run found a clean factorization that the first English run missed. The route itself was better. In the larger study, K3 scored 72 out of 72 in English and 71 out of 72 in Mandarin. Qwen scored 65 out of 72 in English and 62 out of 72 in Mandarin. Mandarin did not improve accuracy.
Creativity is harder to score. Changing the language changed the route, and one Mandarin route was cleaner and more inventive than its English counterpart. But none of the open-ended ideas became a proof, and K3's nominal Mandarin trace was mostly English. I cannot claim that K3 "thinks in Mandarin." I can say that the prompt language changed what came out.
This reminded me of a famous cross-cultural study in which American and Iranian participants retrieved culturally familiar folktales when reading analogous stories, but not unfamiliar ones. The stories available in memory changed which analogy came to mind. A language model is not a person raised on folktales, but different languages may activate different examples and associations. English remained our default for correctness. For creativity, another language is a cheap perturbation. I would not trust the result more. I would expect it to be different.
The Model Learned Memory, Not Judgment
Published mathematics records ideas that worked. A mathematician also remembers years of ideas that did not. This negative knowledge is part of mathematical taste, and most of it never appears in a paper.
Our archive contained that failed work, so we built a 3,742-example corpus and fine-tuned a private Gemma 4 12B adapter on the project's definitions, proved lemmas, failed routes, and status labels. The data tracked provenance, confidence, and the difference between "proved," "useful as labeled," "representation checked," and "still open." Without those labels, the archive would teach confusion.
The adapter raised project recall from about 0.27 to 0.39 and recall of recent K3 work from about 0.36 to 0.79. But the false-promotion rate worsened from about 0.73 to 0.76, and source-specific synthesis remained at zero. It learned more memory, not better judgment. We didn't promote it for theorem work.
Lean Made the Hidden Assumptions Visible
A separate project gave me a different view of the same models. It used Lean, a proof assistant, to formalize a note in additive combinatorics — the kind of argument where a phrase like "by standard arguments" can quietly hide the entire difficulty.
Lean does not allow that. A missing hypothesis cannot disappear into standard arguments; it has to become a proof, a stated assumption, or a named dependency. Formalizing the note exposed several real problems the prose had glossed. A lemma used a boundedness hypothesis without ever stating it. Some weights needed to be normalized, not merely nonnegative. A coefficient case the prose had skipped needed its own separate branch. Each of those findings led to a correction in the paper.
This environment suited agents well. They could decompose a large route into small targets, search the Mathlib library, compile, and use the error messages to choose the next step. When no single theorem existed for a step, they assembled it from smaller pieces, and completed work could contain no escape hatches — no sorry, no admit, nothing left unproved. Early agents aimed too broadly and declared surfaces checked too soon; we retreated to smaller statements with explicit hypotheses. Prove small things that compile.
But Lean checks only the theorem you actually stated. A valid formal proof can still rest on assumptions stronger than the prose implied, or certify only a stripped-down model of the real claim. In the geometry project, a hidden uniformity failure could take days to find; in Lean, many such errors failed immediately. The roles stayed the same either way: a model proposes, a human decides whether the statement matters, Lean checks the formal claim, and a specialist decides whether it says something useful.
The Archive Had to Remember Failure
A research archive contains facts, guesses, objections, superseded drafts, numerical hints, and failed arguments. A model does not know that a polished paragraph from June 18 was killed by a one-line calculation on June 19. If both enter the prompt, the more fluent passage may win.
We gave each component a source, status, and confidence level. Failed arguments became negative examples. Numerical results stayed numerical. Literature theorems kept their original hypotheses.
Fugu Ultra, Grok, Muse, Gemini, and rotating reviewers compared high-risk records with their sources. They found scope mismatches and stale summaries. They did not certify truth.
Retrieval answers "what is in the archive?" It does not answer "what is true?"
What Actually Worked
We counted progress only when a claim survived source checks, deterministic tests where available, and hostile review. Literature facts needed sources, calculations needed reproducible certificates, and numerical results needed the code and parameters that produced them. Failed routes stayed in the record.
That sounds bureaucratic until a model confidently rediscovers the same dead argument for the fifth time.
Long runs wrote receipts as they went, including the prompt, completed cases, artifacts, and failure point. I learned to distrust any summary without underlying evidence. An agent might report that a model had "cleared" a proof when the response was empty, truncated, or aimed at a different statement.
Long context often hurt. Compact problem maps containing the exact target, legal identities, failed routes, and missing lemma worked better. Parallel models helped when they had different jobs. Asking ten models whether a proof was correct often produced ten summaries of the same hidden mistake.
The most common error was a hidden upgrade: fixed became uniform, termwise became summed, averaged became pointwise, or a simplified model became the original problem.
Models were strongest at the beginning and end of an argument. The missing mathematics sat in the middle, where a limit had to be uniform or an error term had to keep its sign. "Standard elliptic estimates now give the result" often concealed the whole problem.
"Be skeptical" produced skeptical prose. Asking whether a constant was uniform or a transformation preserved the assumptions produced a mathematical audit.
Human review could not wait until the end. AI increased the volume of candidate mathematics, making selection and custody more important.
The Machine Searches. The Mathematician Chooses.
In an earlier essay, "Heaven and Earth," I argued that machines handle the middle of a workflow while the human handles both ends. The human decides what is worth doing, the machine helps produce it, and the human judges whether the result is actually good. The machine can optimize, but the objective function comes from somewhere else.
Mathematics made those ends visible. Guofang chose the problem. Later, humans chose the worthwhile generalization, the relevant missing lemma, and whether a correct argument was worth publishing. Lean could check the theorem we stated, but not whether we stated the right theorem. AlphaEvolve could optimize our evaluator, but not whether it captured the mathematics.
The machine's middle was larger than I expected: literature review, translation across fields, conjecture generation, calculation, counterexample search, formalization, criticism, and manuscript production. The human role shifted toward choosing, steering, compressing, and judging.
Powerful tools create more accessible problems, not fewer. The 84-minute calculation opened a general-domain problem and then a harder follow-up. Each answer exposed questions that had previously been too expensive to ask.
Breadth and Translation
Machines were excellent at literature review and at translating ideas between fields. A theorem with different notation and vocabulary might share the same logical shape as our problem.
We gave Manus Wide Research roughly 50 subagents, one per mathematical subfield or related variant, and asked them to find problems with the same logical shape as ours. Some results overstated the literature, and every serious candidate needed a primary-source check. But the search covered more territory than one person could, showing which mechanisms had analogues and where their hypotheses failed. It found no theorem we could simply import.
A human specialist has deep knowledge of a few neighborhoods. A machine can move quickly across many, though shallowly.
Computation and Counterexamples
Agents could expand formulas, test parameter regimes, diagonalize finite models, write symbolic checks, and run brute-force searches without fatigue. Often the fastest route to knowledge was simply to calculate.
Counterexample search may be one of the strongest applications. A lemma can sound inevitable until a program finds a three-variable witness against it. AlphaEvolve and ordinary brute-force code killed intermediate ideas and exposed illegal parameter regimes. The first question can now be: what is the smallest search that could kill this? A counterexample shows which assumption the next theorem must use.
The best outputs were small and checkable: a formula, witness, identity, or finite certificate. The more essay-like the output, the harder it was to know what had been established.
Persistence and Negative Knowledge
A machine will continue down a logical path long after a mathematician would abandon it. A person senses that the signs will never line up or that the lemma is wrong. If the route remains syntactically available, the machine keeps going. This can waste hours, but it can also reveal exactly where a route breaks, uncovering an identity, obstruction, or weaker theorem along the way.
Frontier models have absorbed published mathematics, which mostly records what worked. Papers remove the false starts, failed substitutions, and months spent with the wrong sign. The training corpus contains far more positive than negative knowledge.
A mathematician has lived through failed attempts. She recognizes a familiar dead end before she can always explain why. She knows which arguments lose uniformity and which technically correct lemmas point away from the real structure. This negative knowledge is a large part of mathematical taste. The model has the record. The mathematician has lived through the attempts.
Based on this realization, I fine-tuned Gemma 4 to act like a geometer highly experienced in this area, and that also yielded some insights, although that work is not yet mature enough to give a full account.
A Proof Is Not Yet an Explanation
AI tended to write proofs in the order it discovered them. If three sections used the same idea, it produced three parallel arguments instead of extracting a common lemma. It gave easy algebra and difficult conceptual transitions similar weight.
The result could be correct and useful while remaining unintuitive. Asking the model to shorten it often hid details instead of finding a simpler argument.
The coauthors found repeated proofs, inconsistent notation, definitions after use, and misplaced technical material. They looked across several propositions and recognized one organizing idea. The machine saw legal steps. The mathematicians saw a proof that needed a different shape.
This went beyond writing. Guofang's exponential-decay observation unified cases that the AI had handled separately. Hien's reconstruction was both editorial and mathematical.
Knowing that a statement was true and having a path was valuable. But the first AI proof was rarely the proof a mathematician would keep. It was longer, less motivated, and less revealing. Models could explain narrow questions and execute a human simplification across dozens of pages. They did not reliably step back, see the paper through a reader's eyes, and replace several correct pages with one idea.
Filling Mathematical Potholes
I expect many near-term successes. Some open problems lay fallow while useful tools developed in other fields. Literature-scale search makes them attractive targets.
False conjectures are another source of low-hanging fruit. Agents can search far more configurations than a person would tolerate and turn doubt into an explicit witness. We will see neglected transfers completed, missing cases calculated, and false statements killed.
That phase may move quickly. Then the easy transfers and searchable counterexamples will be gone. We will reach problems whose missing mechanism is not already hiding elsewhere in the literature.
Our private follow-up feels close to that frontier. The agents have narrowed the problem and killed bad routes. My guess is that the remaining step requires the negative knowledge, economy, and global intuition of a human mathematician. The machines have made that person's job much easier by showing where to look.
The Harder Problem Is Still Open
After eight weeks, one paper, hundreds of model calls, a Lean formalization, evolutionary search, visual experiments, a language study, and a fine-tuned model, the harder problem remains open.
The problem is smaller. We know many routes that do not work and can kill weak ideas quickly.
The first 84 minutes showed what AI can do to mathematical speed. The next eight weeks showed what speed leaves unresolved. The machine handled a larger middle than I expected. Humans still chose the problem and decided what counted as an answer.
Only the Doer Learneth
This project made little business sense. It had nothing to do with Aigora. I did it because I was curious, and I learned more than I could have from a hundred benchmark reports.
I learned how models fail, when parallel agents create diversity, how much context is too much, and why failed ideas must be preserved. I learned that a bad evaluator can be more dangerous than its optimizer, and that models can generate mathematics faster than humans can responsibly absorb it.
Elves, the system I use to run long multi-agent projects, improved because mathematics exposed its weaknesses. Handoffs became sharper, claims acquired sources and statuses, reviewers received different jobs, and long runs left evidence behind. None of that knowledge arrived before the work.
Do not wait for someone else to tell you what these systems can do. They do not know either.
Pick a real problem you care about. Make it hard enough that a fluent answer will not fool you. Put the models to work. Check what they produce. Notice where they fail. Change the system and try again.
Get in the trenches.
